common_name: Black Prince Hens and Chicks (Near-Black Purple Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; color deepens with cool nights and strong light, so avoid shade or crowding.

directions: Plant offsets in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun, setting them directly on the surface rather than burying the crown. Black Prince forms tight rosettes of thick, fleshy leaves in deep burgundy-black with narrow, silvery-ciliate tips, holding its dark color especially well through cool fall and winter weather when many other dark sempervivums fade. Like all hens and chicks, individual rosettes are monocarpic, sending up a single tall flower stalk after several years before dying back, while surrounding offsets continue the clump indefinitely. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and needs sharp drainage above all else, making it a strong choice for rock gardens, troughs, and green roofs.

common_name: Othello Hens and Chicks (Large Bright Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring or fall in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; the long stolons make it easy to divide and spread to new locations.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, lean, gravelly soil in full sun; Othello is a large, vigorous cultivar whose rosettes color a vivid bright red with an even deeper red-purple heart, growing bigger and more saturated in color under strong sun and lean conditions. Offsets form on unusually long, thick stolons, letting daughter rosettes root well away from the mother plant and making the cultivar quick to spread and easy to propagate for troughs, walls, and rock gardens. After several years, a mature rosette sends up a tall stalk topped with red flowers and then dies, while the surrounding colony carries on. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease but will rot quickly if left in standing water.
sources: American Conifer Society companion planting reference

common_name: Silver Angel Hens and Chicks (Cobweb-Haired Lime and Burgundy Sempervivum)

planting.note: Plant small offsets in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; keep foliage dry in winter so the cobwebbing does not trap moisture against the crown.

directions: Press small offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; strong light keeps the rosettes tight and heavily webbed. Silver Angel forms small rosettes in lime green shading to burgundy at the leaf tips, densely covered in fine, cobweb-like silvery hairs that give each rosette the look of a tiny snow-capped hill. It multiplies quickly into a dense mounding carpet of rosettes, making it well suited to trough gardens, crevice plantings, and shallow pans where its texture can be appreciated up close. As with other sempervivums, individual rosettes flower once on a stalk and die after blooming, but the surrounding offsets keep the colony going for years.

planting.note: Plant offsets in gritty, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun; this high-alpine species is especially intolerant of winter wet at the crown.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, lean, mineral soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky, sharply drained slopes of its native central and eastern Alps up to 2,800 meters elevation. Sempervivum wulfenii forms rosettes of smooth, fleshy grey-green leaves with a purple-red base and darker tips, spreading by offsets carried on stout stolons up to four inches long. In summer it sends up a stout stalk to about a foot tall bearing clusters of lemon-yellow star-shaped flowers, a distinctive color among hardy sempervivums that are mostly pink to red-flowered. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter lows well below zero, but demands scrupulous drainage year-round and is best sited in a rock garden, scree bed, or trough rather than average garden soil.
